title: Pose purposeful questions
subtitle: Ask questions that reveal and advance student thinking — not just questions that check whether they got the answer.

sections.sources: Source: NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014) · Adding It Up (2001).

blocks.text: Effective teaching uses purposeful questions to assess and advance students’ reasoning and sense making about important mathematical ideas and relationships.

Questions are how a teacher steers thinking without taking it over. The aim is to **assess** (make current thinking visible) and **advance** (nudge it forward) — while leaving the reasoning with the student. Most classroom questions are neither; they are rapid-fire recall aimed at a single right answer. Purposeful questions are planned in advance and often left hanging with wait time.

rows: “What did you do first?” — surfaces the method.
“Why does that work? How do you know?”
“How does your table connect to the graph?”

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: “Why?” and “How do you know?” as routine questions
Wait time after asking — 5+ seconds of think
Follow-ups that build on the student’s actual answer

no.title: We should *not* see
items: Rapid-fire funneling toward the one answer in mind
The teacher answering their own question after a second
Only recall questions, never reasoning ones

blocks.text: Where it lives in our toolbelt

Purposeful questioning pairs with wait time in [Talk Moves](/math/approach/talk-moves), drives the “monitor” phase of the [5 Practices](/math/approach/five-practices), and is the engine of every [Number Talk](/math/approach/number-talks) and [Error Analysis](/math/approach/error-analysis). The [When to Tell](/math/approach/when-to-tell) guide helps you decide when a question is the right move and when a brief tell is.
Plan two or three questions *before* the lesson — one to surface thinking, one to push it. Then hold your wait time. A planned “how do you know?” beats a dozen improvised “right?”s.
